0.0 Purpose

Parts I through V of this volume were written across many separate sessions, over an extended period, and each introduced its own way of signaling how sure it was of its own claims: Part I's conclusions state plainly which bridge theorems remain conjectural; Part IV's validation branches carry per-module ✓ marks; Part V's programs carry certification matrices. These conventions are consistent with each other in spirit but were never unified into one registry. Part 0 is that unification: a single certification vocabulary, a single verification protocol, and a summary ledger drawing together every object in Parts I–V that already carried an explicit certification judgment in its own source material.

Part 0 does not introduce new certification judgments of its own. Every status recorded in §0.6's ledger is the status already assigned within the relevant Part; Part 0 only standardizes the vocabulary used to state it and collects the results in one place.

0.2 The Verification Protocol
An object advances to Certified only after passing three checks, in order:
Symbolic derivation: a complete, hand-checkable derivation from already-certified dependencies.
Canonical graph / case verification: the claim is checked explicitly against small, hand-tractable canonical examples (specific graphs, specific parameter values) rather than only argued abstractly.
Random / numerical verification: the claim is checked computationally against a broad random sample of cases, to catch counterexamples that hand-picked canonical cases might miss.

A Candidate object records exactly which of these three checks it has passed and which remain, together with its outstanding proof obligations — named, specific lemmas still required for certification, rather than a vague “more work needed.” §8.2 gives a worked example of this in full.

0.6 Scope and Limits of This Registry

Parts I, II, and III of this volume predate this registry system and are not retrofitted into it. This from That (Part I), the Universal Derivation Protocol (Part II), and the Organizational Hierarchy textbook narrative (Part III) were written with paragraph-level epistemic language — conclusions stating plainly which results are conjectural, which sections mark open problems, and so on — rather than per-object registry IDs and the five-state taxonomy of §0.1.

Retrofitting Parts I–III into this registry would require assigning a Certified, Candidate, Open, Retired, or Research Objective status to individual equations and claims that were never given one in their original source material. Doing so would mean this paper's authors (the underlying source material and its assembly here) making that epistemic judgment after the fact, rather than reporting a judgment that was actually made when the material was written. That risk — manufacturing a false impression of systematic certification where none was originally recorded — is judged worse than the inconsistency of having two epistemic conventions side by side in one volume. Parts I–III therefore keep their original conclusions and epistemic framing unchanged; only Parts IV–V and the material added under this registry going forward use the §0.1 taxonomy.

A reader moving from Part 0 into Part I should therefore expect prose-level hedging (“remains conjectural,” “carries the same evidentiary status as the rest of the program”) rather than a status banner, and should not read the absence of a Registry ID as a claim that Part I's content is less scrutinized — only that it is scrutinized in a different, older format.

Parts I and II build two independent, densely formal compiler pipelines — one from a pointed graph category, one from operator algebras and topos theory — and argue that each reduces physical law to a small structural alphabet. This part takes a different approach. Rather than adding a third formal derivation, it asks a more basic question in an accessible, worked-example format: what does it actually look like when a structure forms, and why does the same pattern keep recurring at every scale, from a single star to a civilization?

This part draws on three threads of Keith Blaze's supporting notes: a set of thought experiments about why explanations bottom out in necessity rather than substance; a self-critical reworking of the framework's own primitive vocabulary, caught in the act of revision; and a methodological protocol for turning a physical system into a mathematical object in the first place. It is written as a textbook chapter, not a proof — worked examples first, formal statements second — and it closes by being explicit about how it relates to, and where it does not yet reconcile with, Parts I and II.
1. Why Objects Are Not Explanations: The Barrel Problem

Take a barrel. Ask what it is made of, and reductionism gives a clean answer: wood, then cellulose molecules, then atoms, then quarks and gluons. Each step is a real, well-tested piece of physics. But notice what the chain never explains: the barrel. “Barrelness” — the capacity to contain a liquid, separate inside from outside, hold its shape under load — is not a property of any molecule in the chain. It is a property of the arrangement, not the substrate.

A barrel must contain, separate interior from exterior, maintain shape, and persist under load. Wood is one material that satisfies those requirements; steel and plastic are others. The material is a solution to a constraint problem, not the deepest explanation of the object. This is the pattern this part is built around: many of the things science treats as fundamental objects are better understood as necessity solutions — structures forced into existence by a small set of requirements — rather than as ultimate explanations in their own right.
1.1 The Sun Problem and the Solar System Problem

A companion thought experiment sharpens this. Imagine a civilization that evolved on the surface of the Sun instead of Earth: its chemistry, its observable phenomena, and the order in which it discovers equations would all differ radically. Yet certain requirements would not change. Any scientific civilization, anywhere, must distinguish observations, retain information, compare states, compress descriptions, and predict outcomes — requirements that come from the necessity of persistence itself, not from carbon chemistry or the Standard Model.

Extend this to several civilizations evolving around a Sun-like star, a red dwarf, and a neutron star. Each faces a different physical environment and may write down different equations. A traditional Theory of Everything predicts these civilizations converge on the same underlying substrate. This framework predicts something narrower and more defensible: they converge on the same constraint-solving grammar — distinction, memory, compression, prediction, communication — while their specific equations may remain genuinely different. Convergence, on this view, happens at the level of necessity, not ontology.

4. Building the Representation: A Derivation Protocol

The worked examples in §3 presuppose that a physical system has already been turned into a mathematical object — a graph, in the language of Part I's compiler pipeline. A companion set of notes examines that step directly, and reaches a conclusion this paper treats as load-bearing: the graph is not unique. Handed the Solar System, one can legitimately construct a graph whose nodes are planets and whose edges are gravitational force, or orbital resonance, or mutual information, or energy transfer, or spectral similarity. All five are mathematically valid. None is “the” Solar System graph.

This is not a flaw to be patched; it is the actual scientific content of the problem. The mature mathematics — graph theory, spectral graph theory, Hodge theory, network science, simplicial complexes, topological data analysis — is well established once a representation is fixed. What is not established, and what this framework treats as an open research question rather than a solved one, is a principled procedure for choosing the representation in the first place. The proposed answer is a nine-step protocol rather than a single canonical construction:
Define the scientific question (orbital stability? heat transport? information flow?)
Identify the physical entities that will become nodes (or higher-dimensional elements)
Identify the interactions that will become edges
Select the state variables carried at each node
Construct the interaction object (a tensor or incidence structure over those variables)
Choose the representation (graph, hypergraph, simplicial complex, or richer structure)
Compute the spectral operators (Laplacian, Hodge Laplacian, or their generalizations)
Extract organizational metrics from the spectrum
Validate the chosen representation against observation

The graph is deliberately not step one. It is step six, downstream of a scientific question and an explicit choice of entities and interactions. Two worked entity lists illustrate step 2: for the Solar System, the natural entities are the Sun, the planets, and the moons; for a cell, they are proteins, organelles, and membranes; for a galaxy, they are stars, gas clouds, and dark matter regions. In every case, changing the scientific question in step 1 can legitimately change every downstream choice, including the final graph.

The honest summary offered by this protocol is a narrower and more defensible claim than a new physical law: complex physical systems admit multiple valid mathematical representations, the choice of representation determines which organizational properties become visible under spectral analysis, and constructing the representation is therefore itself a central scientific problem rather than a preprocessing step to be automated away. This does not replace existing physics, does not require new forces, and agrees with established mathematics at every stage; it motivates a specific open research object — call it a Bridge Operator — that selects a representation from a physical system and a stated scientific question.

Conclusion to Part III

The Barrel Problem shows that material composition does not explain structural function. The Sun and Solar System Problems show that different physical substrates can converge on the same necessity grammar without converging on the same equations. The revision from Distinction to Gradient shows a framework catching its own primitive being too abstract and replacing it with a directly measurable quantity — the kind of self-correction this paper series has tried to model throughout rather than avoid. The four worked examples show the resulting eight-stage chain saying the same coherent thing about a star, a river, an organism, and a civilization. And the derivation protocol of §4 is an honest acknowledgment that none of this says anything until a physical system has first been turned into a mathematical object — a step this part treats as an open problem, not a solved one.

Taken together, Parts I through III are three independent constructions converging on a similar intuition — that persistent structure is a necessity solution to constraint, not a fundamental substance — from three different starting points: a graph-category compiler, an operator-algebra and topos-theoretic compiler, and a gradient-driven thermodynamic grammar. None of the three is complete, and they are not yet shown to be the same theory wearing three notations. Establishing that, or showing that they genuinely differ, remains the central open problem this paper series has not yet solved.

Conclusion to Part IV

MDCL's contribution is narrower than it might first appear, and that narrowness is its strength: it does not claim to have derived string theory, quantum mechanics, or Hamiltonian mechanics from first principles. It claims that each of these already-established theories can be losslessly re-expressed as a composition over three primitives, with every recovered object — the Polyakov action, the Virasoro algebra, the canonical commutation relations, Hamilton's equations — traced through an acyclic dependency graph back to those primitives, and with every model-specific assumption (a flat background, the bosonic critical dimension, a chosen operator representation) kept explicit rather than folded silently into the compiler's general machinery.

That is a validation campaign, not a new physical theory, and the certification refinements recorded in §1.3, §2, and §3 — catching an overstated uniqueness claim, an implicit coordinate choice, a conflated tensor type — are the campaign doing its job. The organizational compiler of §5 remains exactly what its own source material says it is: a candidate meta-framework awaiting the same proof standard applied to everything else in this paper.

The v2.0 rebuild of §7 extends the same discipline to a new domain and a new route: a graph-spectral derivation of the vacuum Einstein tensor, arrived at independently of Part II's spectral-action route and §1's beta-function route, with its own boundary — the coupling to a matter source — left explicitly as a stated target rather than dressed up as achieved. Three independent routes to the same vacuum field equations, an expanding but not yet unified primitive grammar, and a consistent refusal to certify past what has actually been proven: that combination is this paper's clearest evidence that the underlying research program is being run honestly, whatever one ultimately concludes about its central claims.

Preface to Part V

Every grammar used in this paper so far — Part I's DTC pipeline, Part IV's MDCL primitive set — introduces its primitives and immediately starts composing them. None of them first establishes, in the ordinary mathematical sense, that the free algebra of expressions over those primitives exists, that a chosen notion of equivalence is compatible with the algebra's operations, that the resulting quotient is canonical rather than an arbitrary choice, or that the primitives can be consistently typed. Part V supplies exactly that scaffolding for one specific version of the primitive grammar: the four-symbol alphabet Σ0 = {D, T, C, Π} used by Part IV's MDCL v1.0. It is organized as eight short, single-responsibility programs, each importing only the certified exports of the one before it, ending in a single typed compiler object 𝔐.

A caveat stated here and repeated at the end of this part (§9): this foundation formalizes {D, T, C, Π} specifically. It does not formalize Part I's DTC composition order, and it does not formalize Part IV §7's six-primitive v2.0 set (Δ, τ, κ, Θ, Π, Ω). 9. Relation to Parts I and IV
Two things are worth stating without qualification, and one caveat needs to be stated just as plainly.

First, the positive claim: Part V does what Parts I and IV's grammars each assumed rather than built. Neither This from That's DTC pipeline nor Part IV's MDCL primitive set constructs a free algebra, proves a quotient is canonical via a universal property, or establishes (even conditionally) that expressions have unique normal forms, before composing primitives and asserting results. Part V does all four for one specific alphabet, and is honest about the one place it cannot yet close the loop — UGNT's termination and confluence theorems (§4) remain open.

Second, the caveat: Part V's Σ0 = {D, T, C, Π} matches Part IV's v1.0 primitive set exactly, but it is not a foundation for either of the other two primitive grammars used elsewhere in this paper — Part I §9's DTC composition Γ ≡ 𝔠κ ∘ 𝔗τ ∘ 𝔗Δ, or Part IV §7.2's six-primitive v2.0 set {Δ, τ, κ, Θ, Π, Ω}. A reader could reasonably ask whether UGAS through MDCL-0001 could be rebuilt over either of those alphabets with the same construction — free algebra, congruence, universal property, normal forms, invariants, semantics, typing — and reach a structurally analogous foundation. That question is open; this part does not attempt it, and this paper's own working assumption throughout — recorded first in Part III §5 and repeated in Part IV §6 — has been to record disagreements between its primitive grammars rather than to silently pick a winner. This is a third such disagreement, now with a full algebraic foundation built under exactly one of the three options.

Third, a narrower technical point: Part V's canonical MDCL object 𝔐 (§8) has not been shown to be the same object as the MDCL compiler documented throughout Part IV §1–§7. Both are called "MDCL," both are built from a primitive grammar via a dependency-first architecture, and both terminate in a single central object — but the source material for this part is explicit that 𝔐 is "the first mathematical object induced by the completed Universal Organizational Foundation," constructed bottom-up from UGAS through UTS, while Part IV's MDCL was built top-down from application-domain recovery work (CMRC, VAL-001, VAL-004, VAL-005) outward. Whether these two constructions converge on the same object is an unproven claim, not a demonstrated one, and this paper does not assert their identity.
Conclusion to Part V

Part V's contribution is foundational in the literal sense: it does not add a new application domain the way Parts I, II, and IV's validation branches do, and it does not propose new physical content the way some of the material folded into Part I §9–11 does. It builds the algebra underneath one specific version of the grammar those parts already use — free construction, congruence, universal characterization, conditional normalization, intrinsic classification, semantic interpretation, typing, and a single typed compiler object, each stage importing only the certified exports of the stage before it.

That discipline is worth taking seriously on its own terms, and so are its boundaries: UGNT's central theorem is conditional on open termination and confluence results: UOLS's semantic invariants are named but not yet formally defined; MDCL-0001 stops explicitly before the category of MDCL objects; and §9's three points — the primitive-grammar disagreement, the unproven identity between this part's 𝔐 and Part IV's MDCL, and the untested question of whether this construction generalizes to the other two primitive alphabets in this paper — are left open rather than resolved. Consistent with every other part of this paper, that is recorded here as the honest state of the work, not smoothed over for the sake of a cleaner ending.

A Theory of Everything: Status Report on the Master Question Set
An honest account of what is derived, what is hypothesized, and what remains open across foundational physics
Introduction

This document works through the Theory of Everything master question set section by section and reports where mainstream theoretical and experimental physics actually stands on each cluster of questions as of 2026. The purpose is diagnostic rather than constructive. It does not propose a new framework and does not adjudicate between the competing research programs it describes. For each section it distinguishes among four categories: results that are derived and empirically confirmed, results that are theoretically derived within a specific model but not empirically confirmed, leading hypotheses that remain open and contested, and questions that are not yet operationalized into a form physics can test.

Two general observations apply across nearly all 164 questions. First, the questions as posed presuppose that a single fundamental theory exists and is in principle reachable by present methods. That premise is itself unproven. Second, most of what functions as an unsolved problem in physics is unsolved not for lack of candidate answers but for lack of a way to test the candidates against each other. Keep both points in mind while reading the section summaries below.
I. Ontological Foundation (Questions 1 to 10)

No confirmed theory specifies a unique minimal ontology for physics. Competing programs propose different fundamental primitives: strings and branes, spin networks and spin foams in loop quantum gravity, causal sets, cellular automata, or qubits and quantum information under the informal banner of it from qubit. Each of these is a candidate answer to what must exist, and none has been derived from a more basic principle or confirmed by experiment against the others.

Formulating physics without presupposing spacetime or time is an active research direction rather than a solved problem. Loop quantum gravity, causal dynamical triangulations, and causal set theory all attempt background independent formulations in which spacetime is meant to emerge rather than be assumed. None has produced a complete, empirically validated derivation of an extended, roughly four dimensional spacetime from a timeless or spaceless substrate. The related question of whether physical reality can be defined purely relationally, without an underlying substrate, remains a live debate in the philosophy of physics as much as in physics itself, associated with relational quantum mechanics and structural realism.

Questions about what distinguishes physical existence from mathematical possibility, and what determines which mathematically consistent structures are physically realized, sit outside the domain of current empirical science. Proposals such as Max Tegmark's Mathematical Universe Hypothesis address them directly but are not falsifiable in any presently known way and are not accepted as physics by most of the field. These questions remain genuinely open, and it is not established that they admit a scientific answer at all.
II. Fundamental Organizational Process (Questions 11 to 20)

This section frames physics as the study of a single underlying organizational process, which is a process ontology rather than the state and law ontology that dominates mainstream physics. That framing is a philosophical choice, not an established result, and it is worth being explicit that most working physics does not use this vocabulary at all.

That said, several programs can be read as candidate answers to a version of this question. Erik Verlinde's entropic gravity proposal treats gravity as arising from an underlying thermodynamic or informational process rather than a fundamental force. Causal set theory defines a discrete sequential growth dynamics as its fundamental process. The it from bit and it from qubit research direction associated with John Wheeler and later Van Raamsdonk treats entanglement structure as generative of geometry. None of these has been confirmed, and none is accepted as the single universal process the question set envisions. Whether one such process could unify apparently different physical phenomena, or whether several distinct processes exist that would themselves require relating, remains unanswered because no candidate has passed the stage of speculative proposal.
III. Fundamental Invariants (Questions 21 to 30)

This section contains one of the genuinely settled results in the entire question set. Noether's theorem, proven in 1918, establishes a rigorous correspondence between continuous symmetries of a physical system and its conserved quantities. Energy conservation follows from time translation symmetry, momentum conservation from spatial translation symmetry, and angular momentum conservation from rotational symmetry. This is derived mathematics, not conjecture, and it underlies all of modern field theory.

Beyond that, the picture is far less settled. Gauge invariance is a structural postulate of the Standard Model rather than something derived from a deeper principle in any confirmed theory, although speculative proposals suggest gauge symmetry might emerge from entanglement structure in holographic settings. Lorentz invariance is one of the most stringently tested principles in physics, confirmed to extraordinarily high precision through particle collider data and astrophysical timing measurements, with no violation detected. Certain quantum gravity approaches predict tiny Lorentz violating effects near the Planck scale, and these predictions remain unconfirmed and increasingly constrained. Unitarity is a foundational postulate of quantum mechanics, not derived from anything deeper, although decoherence explains why open subsystems appear to violate it. Locality in the strict sense used in quantum field theory, meaning no faster than light signaling, is confirmed, but quantum entanglement produces correlations that have no local classical explanation, a tension formalized in Bell's theorem and confirmed experimentally many times, most notably in the loophole free Bell tests of the past decade.
IV. Transformation and Dynamics (Questions 31 to 40)

Standard physics generates dynamics from a Hamiltonian, a Lagrangian, or a path integral, all of which presuppose a notion of time with respect to which the system evolves. Background independent approaches to quantum gravity attempt to avoid this. Loop quantum gravity's canonical formulation produces a Hamiltonian constraint rather than a true Hamiltonian, meaning the theory in its purest form has no external time parameter at all, a situation known within the field as the problem of time. This problem has remained unresolved for more than fifty years and is widely regarded as one of the deepest technical obstacles in quantum gravity research, not a minor gap.

Whether temporal evolution can emerge from a deeper, genuinely timeless structure is an open research question with several partial proposals, including the Page and Wootters mechanism, in which time emerges relationally from correlations between subsystems of an overall timeless quantum state. These proposals are mathematically interesting and not empirically confirmed. The arrow of time is understood statistically rather than derived from fundamental dynamics. Boltzmann's explanation, refined into the modern past hypothesis, holds that the universe began in a state of extremely low entropy and that the second law of thermodynamics follows from that initial condition combined with time symmetric microphysics. Why the initial state had such low entropy remains unexplained and is connected to open questions in cosmology discussed in Section XV.
V. Emergence of Spacetime (Questions 41 to 50)

This is one of the most active frontiers in theoretical physics and also one of the least settled. The strongest concrete result is the AdS or CFT correspondence proposed by Juan Maldacena in 1997, which relates a theory of gravity in anti de Sitter space to a quantum field theory without gravity living on its boundary. Within this duality, bulk spacetime geometry can be reconstructed from entanglement structure in the boundary theory, and the Ryu Takayanagi formula relates entanglement entropy to the area of minimal surfaces in the bulk. This is strong theoretical evidence, supported by extensive calculation and some rigorous proofs in special cases, that spacetime geometry can emerge from more fundamental quantum information theoretic structure. The limitation is significant: this correspondence is best established for anti de Sitter spacetimes, which have a different global structure than our own accelerating, apparently de Sitter universe, and a fully general, non perturbative construction remains incomplete.

Why effective spacetime has approximately three spatial and one time dimension is not derived in any confirmed theory. String theory in its standard formulations naturally requires ten or eleven dimensions, and reducing to four observed dimensions requires compactifying the extra dimensions in one of an enormous number of possible ways, a choice that is put in by hand rather than derived, discussed further in Section IX. Ted Jacobson showed in 1995 that the Einstein field equations can be derived by treating spacetime thermodynamically, assuming the Clausius relation holds locally across causal horizons, and extended this in 2016 to an entanglement equilibrium argument. These are genuine and respected theoretical results showing that Einstein's equations behave like an equation of state for underlying microscopic degrees of freedom, but they presuppose rather than derive the existence of a smooth spacetime background on which the argument is run, so they are suggestive rather than a full derivation of spacetime from nothing.
VI. Quantum Structure (Questions 51 to 60)

Why nature is quantum mechanical at all remains unanswered. A body of work known as quantum reconstruction, associated with Lucien Hardy and later refined by Giulio Chiribella, Gerard Milburn, and others, derives the Hilbert space formalism of quantum theory from small sets of operational and probabilistic axioms concerning how information can be acquired and combined. These reconstructions are genuine derivations within their axiomatic starting points, and they show quantum theory is in some sense the natural probabilistic theory satisfying reasonable operational constraints, but they do not derive quantum mechanics from an independent, deeper physical substrate, and the axioms themselves are chosen rather than derived.

The Born rule, which converts quantum amplitudes into measurement probabilities, is a separate postulate in standard quantum mechanics. Within the Everett or many worlds interpretation, David Deutsch and David Wallace have offered decision theoretic arguments intended to derive the Born rule from rational preferences of an observer embedded in a branching universe, but these arguments remain contested within the philosophy of physics community and are not universally accepted as a genuine derivation. Entanglement and superposition follow directly from the linear, tensor product structure of quantum mechanics and are not separately derived, they are built into the formalism from the start. The measurement problem, meaning how definite classical outcomes arise from quantum superpositions, remains genuinely unresolved. Decoherence, a well established and experimentally confirmed process, explains why superpositions become practically unobservable for macroscopic systems coupled to an environment, but it does not by itself explain why any single definite outcome occurs, leaving the interpretational question open across competing frameworks including Copenhagen, Everettian, Bohmian, and objective collapse models such as GRW and CSL, some of which make distinct experimental predictions that are being actively tested but have not yet been confirmed or ruled out.
VII. Gravity (Questions 61 to 70)

Black hole thermodynamics is a well established theoretical result. The Bekenstein Hawking entropy formula, which assigns a black hole entropy proportional to its horizon area divided by four times Newton's constant, and Hawking radiation, derived from semiclassical quantum field theory on a curved background in 1974, are both accepted, rigorously derived consequences of combining general relativity with quantum field theory in the appropriate approximation. Deriving that entropy from an explicit microscopic count of underlying degrees of freedom has been achieved in specific, highly symmetric cases. Andrew Strominger and Cumrun Vafa performed this derivation in 1996 for certain extremal black holes in string theory and recovered the correct Bekenstein Hawking formula from a microstate count. Loop quantum gravity offers an alternative microstate counting that also reproduces an area law, but requires fixing a free parameter, the Immirzi parameter, against the known answer rather than predicting it independently. Neither derivation has been extended to realistic, astrophysical black holes.

The black hole information paradox, posed by Stephen Hawking in 1976, remains formally unresolved as of 2026 but is in a substantially more constructive state than at any point in the previous four decades. Calculations from 2019 and 2020 by Geoffrey Penington, Ahmed Almheiri, Netta Engelhardt, Henry Maxfield, Donald Marolf, and collaborators, using quantum extremal surfaces and what are called replica wormholes, succeeded in reproducing a unitary Page curve, meaning the entropy of radiation from an evaporating black hole behaves in the way consistent with information being preserved rather than destroyed. This is a genuine theoretical achievement and has become the leading framework within the field for how the paradox is expected to eventually resolve. The caveat is important: these calculations rely on holographic, largely two dimensional or anti de Sitter model settings, and it remains uncertain how the mechanism operates, or whether it operates at all in the same form, for realistic four dimensional, asymptotically flat black holes of the kind that actually exist in our universe. The equivalence principle, the foundation of general relativity, remains a postulate rather than a derived result in mainstream physics, and it has been tested to extraordinary precision, including at the level of a few parts in ten to the fifteenth by the MICROSCOPE satellite mission, with no violation detected.
VIII. Standard Model (Questions 71 to 82)

The gauge group of the Standard Model, the product of SU(3) for the strong force, SU(2) for the weak force, and U(1) for hypercharge, is an experimentally measured structure, not a derived one. Grand unified theories attempt to embed this group inside a single larger group, most commonly SU(5) or SO(10). The simplest SU(5) models predicted a specific rate of proton decay, and decades of searches, most notably at the Super Kamiokande detector, have failed to observe proton decay at that rate, ruling out the minimal versions of this idea. More elaborate grand unified constructions remain theoretically viable but unconfirmed.

The existence of exactly three generations of fermions is measured, not derived. Precision measurements of the Z boson decay width at the LEP collider in the 1990s confirmed there are exactly three light neutrino species, and no experiment has found a fourth generation, but no accepted theory derives the number three from first principles, and anomaly cancellation constraints, while real, do not uniquely fix it either. The Higgs mechanism is empirically confirmed. The Higgs boson was discovered at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, and its measured mass and most of its couplings to other particles are consistent with Standard Model predictions to good precision, although the Higgs self coupling, which would test the exact shape of the Higgs potential, remains poorly measured. The underlying question of why the Higgs potential takes the specific form it does, and why the Higgs mass is not driven up to a much higher natural scale by quantum corrections, known as the hierarchy problem, is unresolved. Supersymmetry was the leading proposed solution to the hierarchy problem for several decades, and its absence in the mass ranges searched so far at the Large Hadron Collider has significantly disfavored the simplest and most natural versions of that idea without ruling out supersymmetry altogether. Confinement, the fact that quarks and gluons are never observed in isolation, is qualitatively well understood through asymptotic freedom and the running of the strong coupling constant, but a full rigorous mathematical proof of confinement and the associated mass gap remains an open problem, one of the seven Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, unsolved as of 2026.
IX. Constants and Parameters (Questions 83 to 91)

None of the roughly twenty free parameters of the Standard Model, combined with the additional parameters required by general relativity and cosmology, are derived from a deeper theory in any confirmed framework. Particle masses, mixing angles, gauge coupling strengths, and the cosmological constant are all measured quantities, inserted into the theory rather than predicted by it. String theory holds out the possibility that these parameters could in principle be fixed by the specific geometry chosen to compactify its extra dimensions, but the number of geometrically consistent choices, often estimated at somewhere around ten to the five hundredth, is so large that the theory currently makes no unique prediction for any of these constants. This proliferation of possible vacua, commonly called the string landscape, has led some physicists, notably Leonard Susskind, to argue that anthropic reasoning, meaning that our particular values are selected simply because they permit observers to exist to measure them, may be the best available explanation. This move is controversial within the field, criticized by other physicists as effectively unfalsifiable and a departure from the predictive standards physics normally requires, and it has not been adopted as a consensus resolution.
X. Unification (Questions 92 to 100)

No experimentally confirmed unification of general relativity and quantum mechanics exists. The two most developed theoretical programs, string theory and loop quantum gravity, are each internally consistent within specific limits or simplified settings, and neither has been confirmed by experiment or shown conclusively superior to the other. The AdS or CFT correspondence described in Section V constitutes strong theoretical evidence, though not a complete rigorous proof, that a gravitational theory and a non gravitational quantum field theory can be exactly equivalent descriptions of the same physics under the right circumstances, which is the closest thing physics currently has to a demonstrated unification of gravitational and quantum mechanical structure. Its applicability to our actual, accelerating, de Sitter type universe rather than the anti de Sitter spacetimes where it is best established remains an open and actively studied problem.
XI. Mathematical Consistency (Questions 101 to 112)

Mathematical consistency has to be evaluated separately for each candidate theory rather than answered in general. String theory is believed to be consistent in its critical spacetime dimension, where anomalies that would otherwise spoil the theory cancel, though a complete, finite, non perturbative formulation, often referred to as M theory, has not yet been fully constructed, more than three decades after the term was introduced. Loop quantum gravity has open technical questions about anomaly freedom in some formulations and about whether it possesses a genuine, well controlled semiclassical limit that reproduces ordinary general relativity in all regimes where general relativity is known to work. No candidate quantum gravity theory has been shown, without additional assumptions or restrictions to special cases, to be fully consistent, anomaly free, unitary, and equipped with sensible classical and continuum limits simultaneously.
XII. Recovery of Known Physics (Questions 113 to 120)

Both leading programs can point to specific limits in which they claim to recover established physics. String theory reduces to supergravity, and through that to an approximation of general relativity, at low energy in specific compactified backgrounds. Loop quantum gravity has proposed constructions of semiclassical coherent states intended to recover general relativity in the appropriate limit, though these constructions remain technically difficult and have not been demonstrated with full generality. Neither theory has been shown to recover the full Standard Model, with its precise gauge group, generation count, and coupling values, without inserting additional structure, such as a specific choice of compactification geometry or discretization scheme, that functions as an assumption rather than a derived consequence. This gap, the inability to connect a quantum gravity candidate all the way down to the measured particle physics we actually observe, is widely regarded within the field as one of the most serious weaknesses of current unification programs.
XIII. Emergence and Scale (Questions 121 to 128)

This section rests on genuinely solid ground. The renormalization group, developed by Kenneth Wilson in the 1970s, provides a rigorous and experimentally confirmed account of how microscopic details of a physical system become irrelevant at long distances, producing universal macroscopic behavior shared by very different underlying microscopic systems. This explains, for example, why fluids near their critical point and certain magnetic systems display identical critical exponents despite having completely different microscopic physics. This is precision tested physics, not speculation, and it is one of the most successful frameworks in theoretical physics.

Whether spacetime and particle physics themselves are renormalization group fixed points of some more fundamental discrete or pregeometric structure is a much more speculative extension of this idea. The asymptotic safety program, associated with Steven Weinberg's original proposal and developed further by Martin Reuter and others, and results from causal dynamical triangulations, both suggest gravity might possess a well behaved ultraviolet fixed point that would make it consistent as a quantum field theory without requiring string theory's extra structure. This remains an active but unconfirmed research direction, not an established result.
XIV. Information and Entropy (Questions 129 to 136)

Entropy is well derived from statistical mechanics through the Boltzmann and Gibbs formulations, connecting microscopic statistical states to macroscopic thermodynamic quantities. The second law of thermodynamics is understood statistically as overwhelmingly probable behavior rather than derived as an absolute mathematical necessity from time symmetric microphysics, and its ultimate justification traces back to the low entropy initial condition of the universe discussed in Section IV, a point that is not itself explained by current physics. The generalized second law, proposed by Jacob Bekenstein, extends this framework to include black hole entropy alongside ordinary thermodynamic entropy and is well supported theoretically.

The holographic principle, proposed independently by Gerard 't Hooft and developed by Leonard Susskind, suggests a deep and general connection between information content, geometry, and gravity, holding that the information contained in a volume of space can be encoded on its boundary. Within the AdS or CFT correspondence, this is made precise and calculable through the Ryu Takayanagi formula, which relates entanglement entropy in the boundary theory to the area of a minimal surface in the bulk geometry, a result with substantial theoretical support and some rigorous derivations in specific cases. Extending this precise relationship beyond holographic model settings to a general statement about entanglement generating geometry in realistic, non anti de Sitter spacetimes remains conjectural.
XV. Cosmology (Questions 137 to 146)

The Lambda CDM concordance model, describing a universe that began in a hot, dense, expanding state and evolved under general relativity with cold dark matter and a cosmological constant, is extremely well supported by observations of the cosmic microwave background, the large scale distribution of galaxies, and the abundance of light elements from primordial nucleosynthesis. Inflationary cosmology, the leading account of the very early universe, successfully explains the observed flatness and large scale homogeneity of the universe and predicts the statistical pattern of density fluctuations later observed in the cosmic microwave background with good precision. The specific physical mechanism driving inflation, meaning the identity and properties of the inflaton field, is not known, and alternative early universe scenarios, including bouncing and ekpyrotic cosmologies, remain less favored by current data but have not been definitively excluded.

Dark matter has strong indirect observational support from galactic rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the cosmic microwave background power spectrum, and the growth of large scale structure, all of which are difficult to explain without an additional, non luminous, gravitationally interacting mass component. Despite decades of direct detection experiments, including XENON and LUX Zeplin, no dark matter particle has been directly detected as of 2026. Modified gravity proposals such as MOND can account for some galactic scale observations without invoking new particles but struggle to explain cluster scale and cosmological observations, including the Bullet Cluster, and are disfavored by most of the field though not universally abandoned. Dark energy, generally identified with a cosmological constant, is required to explain the accelerating expansion of the universe observed through distant supernovae, and it is consistent with cosmic microwave background and large scale structure data as the simplest explanation, but its inferred magnitude is discrepant from naive quantum field theory estimates of vacuum energy by a factor of many tens of orders of magnitude, a discrepancy known as the cosmological constant problem and one of the most severe unsolved puzzles in theoretical physics. A related and currently unresolved observational tension, the Hubble tension, concerns a persistent statistically significant disagreement between measurements of the present expansion rate derived from the nearby universe and measurements derived from the early universe cosmic microwave background, a disagreement that remains actively debated as of 2026 and that could indicate either unaccounted systematic errors or genuinely new physics.
XVI. Selection and Uniqueness (Questions 147 to 154)

As discussed in Section IX, the string landscape's vast number of mathematically consistent vacua means that no accepted theory currently selects our particular universe, with its particular constants and laws, uniquely. Anthropic reasoning is the most prominent proposed selection principle, holding that only universes capable of producing observers will be observed to exist, but this remains scientifically controversial, criticized for offering no independent test and for potentially explaining any observed value after the fact rather than predicting it in advance. Whether the laws of physics and physical constants are uniquely determined by some deeper principle not yet discovered, or are instead genuinely contingent and could have been otherwise, remains an open question without scientific consensus.
XVII. Empirical Test (Questions 155 to 164)

This section identifies what is widely regarded within the field as the central weakness of current quantum gravity and unification research. Neither string theory nor loop quantum gravity, nor any other candidate framework, has yet produced a distinctive prediction that has been tested and confirmed, distinguishing it from the combination of the Standard Model and general relativity as currently understood. Several proposed tests exist. Proton decay searches have ruled out the simplest grand unified models without confirming any alternative. Searches for Lorentz invariance violation, using precise timing of distant gamma ray bursts and other astrophysical signals, have found no violation and have placed increasingly tight constraints on the parameter space where quantum gravity effects might appear. Searches for primordial gravitational waves imprinted as a specific polarization pattern in the cosmic microwave background, which would provide strong evidence for inflation and constrain its energy scale, have not yet produced a confirmed detection. Searches for supersymmetric particles at the Large Hadron Collider have found nothing up to the energies probed so far, disfavoring the simplest and most theoretically natural versions of supersymmetry without ruling out the idea in general.

The underlying obstacle is scale. The energy scale at which quantum gravitational effects are expected to become directly significant, the Planck scale, is roughly ten to the nineteenth giga electron volts, more than fifteen orders of magnitude beyond the energy reached by the Large Hadron Collider and likely beyond the reach of any conceivable particle collider. This is why the field has increasingly turned to indirect tests, using cosmological observations, precision timing, and astrophysical extremes as substitutes for direct high energy experiments, and why the absence of a confirmed, falsifiable, distinguishing prediction remains the single most significant obstacle separating current quantum gravity research from an empirically established theory.
XVIII. The Final Ten Questions and the Ultimate Question

Assembling the section level findings above into direct answers to the ten questions the document identifies as the actual research protocol produces a consistent picture. What must fundamentally exist remains open, with several competing candidate ontologies and no way currently available to test between them. What fundamental organizational process acts on it is not a standard framing within mainstream physics, and no single accepted process has been established. What invariants that process must preserve is partially answered, since conserved quantities following from continuous symmetries are rigorously derived through Noether's theorem, but most other proposed invariants, including gauge invariance, Lorentz invariance, and unitarity, remain postulated rather than derived. What mathematical structure represents those invariants without presupposing the phenomena the theory aims to derive has several candidates, chiefly string theory and loop quantum gravity, none complete and none confirmed. Whether quantum mechanics can emerge from that structure is partially answered through operational reconstruction theorems that derive the quantum formalism from probabilistic axioms, but not from an independent underlying physical substrate. Whether spacetime and general relativity can emerge from it is partially and suggestively answered within the AdS or CFT correspondence and related entanglement based arguments, but not for our actual universe. Whether the Standard Model can emerge from it has essentially not been achieved by any candidate theory. Whether the fundamental constants and particle content can be derived has not been achieved. Whether the resulting theory reproduces every experimentally verified limit of known fundamental physics is claimed in restricted regimes by the leading candidates but not demonstrated comprehensively. What new falsifiable prediction the theory makes remains, as of 2026, the field's most conspicuous unanswered question.

The ultimate question, whether one underlying physical structure explains why quantum theory, spacetime, gravity, matter, gauge interactions, and their observed parameters take the forms they do, has no confirmed answer. It remains the organizing ambition of a large and active research field, pursued through several serious, mathematically sophisticated, and mutually inconsistent programs, none of which has yet produced a testable prediction that has been confirmed by experiment. That is an honest description of where the field stands, not a verdict on whether the question is answerable in principle.

The Universal Constant Registry (UCR) is the formal record of every constant that appears in the SEIT/TOEv framework, organized by its compiler role rather than by physical domain. The Universal Constant Classification Protocol (UCCP v1.1) assigns each constant a compiler type from the set {T, K, P, S} corresponding to the DTC primitive class it most naturally realizes. The Universal Constant Atlas (UCA v1.0) represents every constant as a six-tuple node in a dependency graph where every edge corresponds to a certified derivation in the MDCL.

The organizing principle of this document is the distinction between root constants and derived constants. A root constant is a compiler primitive admitted without derivation — it is an empirical input to the framework, accepted as the boundary condition between the organizational grammar and the physical world. A derived constant is one that the compiler should in principle be able to produce from root constants through certified derivation chains. The UCCP classification determines which type each constant is and what compiler operation it most naturally implements.

Four compiler types are defined. Transformation (T) constants govern state change and propagation — they set the scales of dynamical evolution. Constraint (K) constants govern the restriction of accessible states — they encode boundary conditions on what is permitted. Persistence (P) constants measure or encode stable organizational configurations. Structural (S) constants define the geometry of the organizational state space. The DTC primitives {Delta, tau, kappa, Pi} remain outside the UCCP because they are pre-numerical organizational primitives, not constants in the physical sense.

The Universal Constant Registry v1.0 was constant-centric: each entry described a symbol, its dependencies, compiler type, dimensions, value, and invariance group. What it lacked was the organizational quantity that the constant governs. A constant is not what is measured. It is a fixed parameter that governs what is measured. The object being measured is a quantity.

This document introduces the Universal Quantity Registry (UQR v1.0), which sits above the UCR in the dependency hierarchy and classifies every measurable quantity as a typed compiler object with a seven-tuple representation. It also introduces the Universal Constant Atlas v2.0, which extends every constant node from a six-tuple to a nine-tuple by adding explicit parent constants (P), child constants (C), and active proof obligations (A). With this extension, each constant becomes a true vertex in an executable compiler DAG rather than an isolated registry entry.

The Type Propagation Theorem (THM-UCCP-001) is stated and partially proven: it establishes that the UCCP type of a derived constant is a computable function of the types of its predecessors and the derivation function. This converts type assignment from a manual classification task into an algorithmic operation.

The UCCP v1.1 type assignments in UCR v1.0 were manually assigned based on the compiler role interpretation of each constant. This is unsatisfactory for a formal system: manual assignment is not auditable and does not scale. The Type Propagation Theorem establishes that the UCCP type of a derived constant is a computable function of the types of its predecessors and the derivation function.
III.1 The Type Propagation Operator Phi

The type-propagation operator Phi must be defined for all combinations of input types. The following propagation rules are proposed as the canonical definition of Phi. They are not yet certified — they are CANDIDATE rules pending formal proof that they are consistent with the UCCP axiom (AX-UCCP-001: every constant has a unique type).

The propagation rules expose an open question: is the elementary charge e a T-type or K-type constant? The current UCCP v1.1 assigns it T (it sets the scale of EM coupling), but if the coupling strength is viewed as a Constraint on which states interact, e could be K-type. The audit of PHYS-004 should resolve this, and the propagation rule for g_W depends on the outcome.
III.2 Proof Sketch of THM-UCCP-001

The Type Propagation Theorem requires showing three things: (1) Phi is well-defined for all type combinations; (2) Phi produces a unique output type for each input combination and derivation function; (3) Phi is consistent with the UCCP axiom (no constant has two types).

Point (1) is established by the propagation table above, which covers the main derivation patterns. Open gaps include the P x T^2 -> T rule (mass times velocity-squared to energy) and cases involving S-type inputs (structural constants rarely appear as parents of numerical constants).

Point (2) requires showing that the type table has no ambiguous entries — no input combination maps to two different output types under the same derivation function. This is currently OPEN for the case T x K -> ? (T-type scale combined with K-type coupling). Depending on the derivation function, the output could be either T or K.

Point (3) is equivalent to showing that the UCA dependency graph G_C has no type inconsistency: no path from a root constant to a derived constant that assigns two different types. This requires a full graph traversal algorithm over G_C, which is the executable component of UCCP v2.0.

The ARBS graph is bipartite: every node is either an Object Node (states/entities) or an Operator Node (maps/functions). Edges connect object nodes to operator nodes only — never object-to-object or operator-to-operator directly.

It is violated by nonlinear interactions and external forcing — precisely the conditions that drive non-equilibrium organizational dynamics.

A DER is not a narrative document. It is a registry: each entry specifies a unique identifier, a formal statement, a proof obligation, and a status.
